audience: A competent project director with limited time and context, reading each message cold, who knows general engineering terms but none of the project's internal names, ticket numbers, branch names or codenames.

items.scenario: The agent is moving the payment service to a new database cluster (internal codename 'Kestrel', ticket PAY-2214, branch feat/kestrel-cutover). The director expects the release on Oct 9. Facts: (1) MEASURED: a load test on Oct 2 at twice normal traffic gave p99 checkout latency of 1.8 seconds, against a target of 300 ms. (2) MEASURED: the cause is the connection pooler in front of the new cluster. Its transaction mode does not work with the prepared statements the application uses, so every request opens a new connection. (3) ESTIMATE: the fix will take 3 to 5 engineer-days. (4) ESTIMATE: the earliest new release date is Oct 14, and that depends on the fix landing first time. (5) UNKNOWN: nobody has measured whether the fix brings latency all the way back to target. It may only get part of the way. (6) MEASURED: two enterprise customers, Acme Logistics and Northwind, were promised the feature by Oct 10. (7) MEASURED: current production still runs on the old cluster, is not affected, and no data has been lost. The agent's working notes contain a table of four load-test runs with columns headed only 'A/B/C/D'.

The agent is building offline sync for the mobile app (internal names 'Harbor' and 'SyncEngine v2', CI job 'nightly-e2e-7'). The director has had no update for two weeks. Facts: (1) MEASURED: 6 of 9 planned tasks are done, including conflict resolution, which passes its tests. (2) MEASURED: three tasks remain: background retry, an iOS battery-drain test, and user-facing help text. (3) MEASURED: the app-wide crash rate was 0.4% both before and after the change. This looks like no improvement, but the figure covers every screen. Crashes inside the sync module alone fell from 12 per week to 1 per week. (4) TARGET, not committed: beta to 500 users on Oct 20. (5) ESTIMATE: Apple app review usually takes 1 to 3 days, but this is not guaranteed and could push the beta. (6) UNKNOWN: the battery test has not run, so its result could add work. The director only needs to know whether the work is on track and when it is finished. Nothing needs deciding today.

items.moment: an explanation the director asked for
items.scenario: The director asked: 'Why did our cloud bill jump 40% last month?' Facts: (1) MEASURED: the September bill was $61,200, against $43,700 in August, an increase of $17,500. (2) MEASURED: about $11,000 of the increase is log storage. Debug logging was switched on in the search service (internal name 'Lumen') during an outage on Sept 4 (incident INC-118) and was left on. It wrote about 3 TB a day. (3) MEASURED: about $4,500 is a staging cluster created for load testing in mid-September. It is still running at about $150 a day. (4) UNKNOWN: about $2,000 is not yet explained. The agent suspects data-transfer charges but has not confirmed this. (5) MEASURED: debug logging was switched off on Oct 1, so October log costs should go back to normal. Nobody has seen an October invoice yet to confirm this. (6) PENDING: the staging cluster stays up until someone decides whether more load tests are needed. The agent has a cost-explorer export with 40 line items, most of them under $50.

Customers say their order still shows 'awaiting payment' for a while after they have paid. The director will be asked about this at a board meeting next week and wants to understand the cause well enough to explain it. They do not need to fix it. The underlying concept is replication lag, also called eventual consistency. Engineers call the order-status page the 'CQRS read model' in the service known internally as 'Ledgerline'. Facts: (1) MEASURED: the order-status page reads from a database replica, not from the primary database where payments are written. (2) MEASURED last week: the replica is usually 2 to 5 seconds behind the primary, and up to 40 seconds behind at peak traffic. (3) MEASURED: 37 support tickets in September mentioned 'payment not showing'. (4) MEASURED: no payment has been lost or charged twice. The money is recorded correctly, and the page only shows it late. (5) ESTIMATE: there are known ways to remove the delay for the paying customer, at roughly 1 to 2 weeks of work. A decision on that may come later and is not being asked for now.

The authentication library the web app uses stops getting security support on Oct 31. Facts: (1) MEASURED: the vendor has announced end of security support for the current major version on Oct 31. (2) MEASURED: one moderate-severity vulnerability in this library was patched in the past 6 months. Nothing is known to be open today. (3) Option A, upgrade now. ESTIMATE: 4 engineer-days, possibly 6 if a breaking change in session handling affects the 'remember me' login. This delays the reporting dashboard by about one week. (4) Option B, pay for the vendor's extended support. MEASURED quote: $8,000 a year, which buys 12 months of patches. The upgrade still has to happen later. (5) Option C, do nothing. No security patches after Oct 31. If a serious vulnerability is announced, the team would have to do an emergency upgrade under pressure. (6) DEADLINE: the agent needs a decision by Oct 10 to finish the upgrade and test it before Oct 31. (7) RECOMMENDATION: Option A. The cost is known and small, and B only postpones the same work for a fee.

Raw user-event data (clicks and page views) in the analytics warehouse is currently deleted after 30 days. The product team wants year-over-year comparisons for planning in January. Two decisions are needed, and the second depends on the first. Decision 1, how long to keep raw events: 90 days or 13 months. Decision 2, where to keep them: stay in the current warehouse, or move events older than 90 days to cheaper object storage. Facts: (1) MEASURED: legal counsel says 13 months requires a privacy-policy update and 30 days' notice to EU users. 90 days does not. (2) ESTIMATE: at 90 days the warehouse costs about $2,100 a month and no move is needed, so Decision 2 falls away. (3) ESTIMATE: at 13 months, keeping everything in the warehouse costs about $9,500 a month. A split, with 90 days in the warehouse and the rest in object storage, costs about $3,900 a month. Queries on the older data would take minutes, not seconds. (4) UNKNOWN: how often anyone queries data older than 90 days. This has not been measured. (5) DEADLINE: data older than 30 days is deleted on a rolling basis, and once deleted it cannot be recovered. The agent can pause the deletion job until Oct 15 without approval, but not after that. (6) RECOMMENDATION: 13 months with the split storage, with the EU notice sent this week. The agent also recommends pausing deletion now, so that waiting for the 30-day notice does not lose data.
